description: Level III audit prep for Houma yards and NDT firms: hull weld NDT plans, Navy and class requirements, liftboat and crane MT, UR Z17. Describe your audit.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting and Class Audit Support in Houma, Louisiana
html:
Houma's yards build Navy auxiliaries, research ships and Gulf workboats, often side by side, and every one of those hulls brings its own inspection paperwork and its own auditor. This page is for yard quality departments, NDT subcontractors and gauging firms in Terrebonne and Lafourche parishes getting ready for a class, government or customer review of their NDT. As ASNT NDT Level III consultants, Atlantis NDT puts the written practice, procedures and qualification files in order and rehearses the audit with your team. Describe the audit you are facing to start.

The Houma Navigation Canal yards

The largest yard in town is Bollinger Houma, on the west bank of the Houma Navigation Canal about 30 miles from the Gulf of Mexico. Bollinger bought it in 2021 as the shipyard division of Gulf Island Fabrication. The site covers 437 acres with 6,750 feet of water frontage and roughly 160,000 square feet of covered fabrication space. Its current new construction includes Towing, Salvage and Rescue ships (T-ATS) for the US Navy and Regional Class Research Vessels for the National Science Foundation and Oregon State University, and the yard lists ocean-class tugs, OPA 90 tank barges, large liftboats, platform supply vessels and multi-purpose support vessels among the types it builds.

Around that anchor sits the wider bayou workboat economy: smaller builders and repair yards, machine and fabrication shops, crane and lifting-gear specialists, and inspection companies that grew up serving offshore oil and gas. Many of those firms have spent decades on commercial work and are now meeting government contract requirements for the first time, or the reverse. That shift, more than anything technical, is what drives most of the audit preparation we see in this area.

One shed, several rulebooks

A Houma yard can have a Navy auxiliary, a research vessel and a commercial tug under construction in the same season. The NDT technician may not notice the difference from one hull to the next, but the paperwork behind each examination comes from a different place.

Hull typeWhere the NDT requirements come fromWho reviews the evidence
Navy auxiliary under a government contractThe contract specification and whatever NAVSEA publications or military standards it invokes, plus class rules where the contract calls for classThe Navy's on-site representatives and, where invoked, the classification surveyor
Research vesselThe owner's specification, class rules, and Coast Guard rules for oceanographic research vessels in 46 CFR Subchapter U where the vessel falls under themOwner's representative, class surveyor, Coast Guard
Offshore supply vessel or liftboatClass rules if classed, and Coast Guard rules for offshore supply vessels in 46 CFR Subchapter LClass surveyor and Coast Guard marine inspector
Towing vessel46 CFR Subchapter M, class rules if classed, and the owner's specificationCoast Guard or a third-party organization, class surveyor
Tank bargeCoast Guard tank vessel rules, class rules if classed, owner's specificationCoast Guard, class surveyor, owner

The practical lesson: your written practice and procedures need a short front section that says, for each kind of contract, which document governs NDT extent, method, acceptance and personnel qualification, and who has the final word when two of them disagree. Without it, technicians fall back on habit, and habit is exactly what auditors sample.

Research and government hulls add a further reviewer: the owner's representative, who often has inspection hold points of their own written into the specification. On those contracts the NDT report is not finished when the technician signs it. It has to reach the owner's representative in the format the specification asks for, against the drawing and weld identities the owner uses, and in time for the hold point to be released. Yards that treat that hand-off as part of the NDT procedure, rather than as an administrative afterthought, have far fewer arguments at delivery.

Weld NDT on new construction: who decides what gets examined

On a classed hull the yard proposes the extent and location of weld examinations in an NDT plan, and the classification surveyor reviews and accepts it. The rules of each society set the minimum, and IACS publishes a recommendation (No. 20) that many societies lean on when setting weld NDT extent, locations and acceptance levels for hull structure. On a government hull, the contract decides whether those rules apply or whether a military standard does. Either way, three questions come up in every yard audit we prepare for:

  1. Can the yard show who wrote the NDT plan and on what basis? A plan with no reference to the rule or contract clause behind it is an easy finding.
  2. Do the examinations actually done match the plan? Auditors pick weld identities off the plan and ask for the reports. Gaps appear when locations change during fabrication and the plan is not updated.
  3. Is the method right for the joint? Ultrasonic examination is replacing radiography on more hull butts and seams, but only with a technique and personnel qualification the surveyor accepts, often after a demonstration on representative joints.

Our Level III audit support for shipbuilding covers yard NDT plans in more depth, and procedure qualification and demonstration covers how a UT technique is proven before a surveyor accepts it. Radiography stays with licensed contractors: Atlantis runs no source work in the US, given 10 CFR Part 34 and Louisiana's Agreement State licensing, although our Level III can audit an RT contractor's procedure and review its images for your yard.

Liftboat legs, cranes and lifting gear

The Houma area builds and repairs a lot of equipment that lifts: liftboat legs and jacking systems, offshore and vessel-mounted cranes, A-frames and davits, and the pedestals and foundations they sit on. The NDT behind this work is mostly magnetic particle and ultrasonic examination of high-strength steel welds, fatigue-prone details and structural members after repair. The documents that govern it vary: class rules for lifting appliances on classed vessels, API standards for offshore cranes where the owner invokes them, the crane manufacturer's instructions, and the owner's own inspection program.

Auditors of this work focus on whether the technician had the right procedure for the material and geometry, whether MT field adequacy was checked on the actual configuration, whether surface preparation was enough to see a fatigue crack, and whether the report gives the next person enough to find the same location again. A firm that inspects cranes for several owners benefits from technique sheets per crane type rather than one general MT procedure.

Repair, conversion and the gauging question

Workboats come back to Houma yards for drydocking, repowering and conversions, and steel renewal decisions turn on thickness readings. If those readings feed a class survey, the gauging firm needs UR Z17 approval from the vessel's society, and the surveyor will normally want to attend or verify the measurements. For Coast Guard-inspected vessels that are not classed, the Coast Guard inspector decides what evidence is acceptable for the drydock or internal structural examination, and a well-documented gauging report makes that conversation shorter.

A gauging firm working these yards should keep, for every survey: the reading locations on a sketch or plan, original scantlings where known, gauge and probe details, coating handling, verification checks against a reference block at the start and end of each shift, and the operator and supervisor names with their qualification. Our UTM operator qualification guide covers what class auditors expect of the people, and the UR Z17 quality manual page covers the system side.

Yards that subcontract their NDT

Many Houma yards do not employ their own NDT staff and hire local inspection companies instead. That does not move the responsibility. The yard's quality system still has to show how it chose the NDT company, how it checked that company's written practice, procedures and certifications, and how it monitors the work. Class surveyors and government representatives will ask the yard, not the subcontractor.

A short subcontractor evaluation file solves most of this: the NDT company's written practice and procedure list, certifications for the technicians assigned, its calibration register, a record of the yard's review, and periodic spot checks. Our page on subcontractor approval audits sets out a workable format, and ship repair yard NDT programs covers the yard's side of the arrangement. Inspection firms on the other end can use the same list to prepare before a yard audits them.

Oilfield inspectors moving into shipyard work

Much of the NDT labor around Houma learned its trade on offshore platforms, pipelines and oilfield equipment. Those technicians bring real skill, but their certification files were built for a different auditor. Three things usually need attention when they move onto hull and naval work.

First, experience. A Level II UT certification earned on pipe wall thickness and plant piping welds tells a shipyard auditor little about plate butt welds, tee joints or the scan plans used on hull structure. The written practice should say what experience counts toward each certification, and the technician's log should show hours on the kind of work they now sign for. Second, procedures. Oilfield procedures often cite API or ASME acceptance criteria; hull work uses class rules or military standards, and a technician who has memorized one set of numbers can misapply them. Short method-specific briefings, recorded in the training file, close that gap. Third, recertification. When a technician joins a new employer, that employer certifies them afresh under its own written practice; the old employer's certificate is history, not a qualification.

The experience log guidance and our SNT-TC-1A hours planner help a quality manager sort out what a transferring technician can and cannot be certified for on day one.

Where Atlantis fits, and where it does not

Atlantis is itself working toward class approval rather than holding it: our UR Z17 applications with Lloyd's Register, ABS and DNV are in progress, with audits under way, and no certificate has been issued, so Atlantis is not class-approved for any service today. Its management system carries ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification; inspection-body and laboratory accreditation (ISO/IEC 17020, 17025) is something Atlantis does not hold. Nor is Atlantis the yard's surveyor, the Navy's representative or a Coast Guard third-party organization. The yard owns its quality system, each employer certifies its own NDT personnel, and the reviewer decides; our job is to make the evidence complete and the procedures sound.

Engagements are led by the company's founder. He is certified ASNT NDT Level III in five methods, namely magnetic particle, penetrant, visual, ultrasonic and radiographic testing, and has worked in the field internationally for more than a decade.

How an engagement runs for a Houma yard or NDT firm

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad. Houma is a day's drive from Houston, so we combine remote document work with site days rather than keeping anyone locally.

  1. Requirement check. We identify every document that governs NDT on the contracts in scope: contract specifications, class rules, Coast Guard subchapters, owner standards.
  2. Document gap review. Written practice, procedures, technique sheets, NDT plans, certification files and calibration register, marked against those documents.
  3. Corrections. We draft the changes; your Level III or quality manager approves and issues them.
  4. Yard visit. We pull weld identities from the NDT plan and trace them to reports, watch a technician perform an examination, and hold a mock audit with your team.
  5. After the audit. We help write corrective actions with root cause and evidence.

What to send us

  • The audit or review notice, and the contract or specification clauses that cover NDT.
  • The NDT plan for one current hull, with the reports that go with it.
  • Your written practice, procedures and technique sheets.
  • Technician certification files, including vision checks, for the people who will be sampled.
  • For subcontracted NDT: your evaluation file for each NDT company you use.
  • For gauging firms: two recent thickness reports and the class checklist if you are applying for approval.

Audit readiness checklist for Houma yards and inspection firms

  • A governing-document matrix per contract type at the front of the written practice.
  • NDT plans that cite their basis and are revised when weld locations change.
  • UT techniques used in place of radiography backed by a demonstration record the surveyor saw.
  • MT technique sheets for lifting appliances by type, with field checks on the actual geometry.
  • Subcontractor evaluation files that show review, not just collection.
  • Thickness reports with locations, verification checks and qualified operator names.
  • Deficiencies tracked to closure; our deficiency tracking for marine shipyards page shows one approach.

faq.q: Our yard builds a Navy auxiliary and commercial tugs. Do we need two written practices?
faq.a: Not necessarily. One written practice can serve both if it states which document governs personnel qualification and NDT on each contract. If the Navy contract invokes a qualification scheme different from SNT-TC-1A, keep those records clearly separate. See written practice development.

faq.q: Who decides how many hull welds get examined on a classed vessel?
faq.a: The class rules set minimums and the surveyor accepts the yard's NDT plan. The yard proposes; the surveyor approves. Atlantis can help draft and justify the plan, but the decision is the surveyor's.

faq.q: Can we use UT instead of radiography on hull butts?
faq.a: Often, if the class society accepts the technique and the personnel. Expect to demonstrate the technique on representative joints and to show qualification records for the operators.

faq.q: We hire a local NDT company. Is their audit our problem?
faq.a: Yes. The surveyor or government representative will ask the yard how it qualified and monitors its NDT subcontractor. Keep an evaluation file. Our subcontractor approval audit page shows what goes in it.

faq.q: Does a gauging firm need class approval to work on Houma workboats?
faq.a: Only when the readings support a class survey; then the vessel's own society must have approved the firm under UR Z17. Coast Guard-only and owner-only gauging is outside that rule, though owners may still ask for an approved firm.
No. Atlantis has applied to Lloyd's Register, ABS and DNV for UR Z17 approval and is in the middle of those audits. No class approval has been issued to Atlantis.

faq.q: Does Atlantis carry out radiography at yards in Louisiana?
faq.a: No. Radiography in the US requires source licensing, so Atlantis leaves it to licensed contractors. As a Level III we can audit the contractor's procedure and review the images.

faq.q: Can Atlantis serve as our Level III?
faq.a: Yes, as an outside agency Level III for SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 programs in UT, MT, PT, VT and RT. For government contracts, confirm first what the contract requires of the Level III. Details: Level III consulting.

faq.q: Do you write welding procedures for the yard?
faq.a: No. The yard's welding engineer writes and qualifies WPSs and PQRs; Atlantis stays on the NDT side. This explainer on welding qualification records shows how they relate to NDT.
Send the audit notice and the NDT clauses of your contract through the contact form, with your written practice if it is handy. You will hear back from Atlantis within one business day.
